name: binkd
why: A FidoNet mailer daemon, a door into the store-and-forward BBS networks of the pre-internet era.

brief.what_it_is: Binkd is a Fidonet mailer that runs over TCP/IP networks, described by its README as an FTN-compatible internet daemon. It moves Fidonet Technology Network (FTN) mail and file traffic between systems using TCP/IP as the transport, in place of the dial-up links these networks originally used. The input is a configuration file (binkd.cfg, per the README) and the network's FTN traffic, and the output is that traffic delivered between nodes over the internet. The README is short and does not walk through the configuration format.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to make efficient use of the TCP/IP protocol suite as a transport layer for FTN-based (Fido Technology Network) networks.
brief.how_it_works: The README says only that binkd uses the TCP/IP protocol suite as a transport layer in FTN networks. It does not describe the protocol or the daemon's internals; the linked manuals would be needed for detail.

commands_seen.context: Clones the source repository (UNIX build path).
Changes into the cloned source directory.
Copies the UNIX makefiles and configure scripts from mkfls/unix/ into the source root.
Runs the configure script to prepare the build.
Dry run that shows what make install would do, as the post-build message recommends checking first.
Installs binkd as root; the post-build message says the default target is /usr/local.
Sets a different install directory before building, per the post-build message.

brief.install_notes: UNIX: clone the repo, copy the files from mkfls/unix/ into the source root, then run ./configure and make. The post-build message says to run make -n install, become root, run make install, and then rename or move /usr/local/etc/binkd.conf-dist so a later install does not overwrite it. Non-UNIX: find the subdirectory for your system and compiler under mkfls/, copy its files to the source root, and run make, nmake, wmake or gmake depending on your compiler. Installation steps in the README: edit the sample binkd.cfg, then run binkd. No accounts or hardware are mentioned.
brief.standout: It is a Fidonet mailer for a store-and-forward network that predates the internet, now carrying that traffic over TCP/IP, and it has a long-lived community with echomail areas, mirrors and manuals in Russian and English.
brief.status: unknown. The GitHub releases page shows no releases. The README gives no release date, version or last-commit date. The README does name a live-looking developer mailing list and bug address, but gives no dates. The linked English manual is for 0.9.2 and is an archive.org copy, and the Russian manual is for 0.9.9.
brief.caveats: The README is thin on configuration and usage, and it does not say how to set up the sample binkd.cfg. It names binkd.cfg in the Installation section but binkd.conf-dist in the post-build message, which is an inconsistency to check. Non-UNIX builds need manual file copying from mkfls/. Linked docs and mirrors are old (web.archive.org snapshot, corbina.net and happy.kiev.ua hosts). I did not see a license statement in the README.
quotes: Binkd is a Fidonet mailer designed to operate via TCP/IP networks.
As a FTN-compatible internet daemon, it makes possible efficient utilization of TCP/IP protocol suite as a transport layer in FTN-based (Fido Technology Network) networks.
fetch_log: https://github.com/pgul/binkd/releases: worked, page reports no releases
Linked docs (FAQ, English manual, Russian manual) not fetched; listed as links only

judge.reason: It offers a tangible way into FidoNet’s store-and-forward BBS network, carrying its old-school FTN traffic over today’s TCP/IP.

entry.title: binkd
entry.tldr: A mailer daemon that carries FidoNet mail and files over TCP/IP, a way to touch the store-and-forward BBS networks that predate the internet.
entry.deeper_look:
binkd is a mailer for FTN, the Fido Technology Network family, which includes FidoNet. These networks grew up around dial-up bulletin board systems. Each system collected mail and files, then called a neighbour on a schedule to hand them on. Nobody needed a permanent connection, and messages hopped from node to node until they arrived.

binkd keeps that model and swaps the transport. The README describes it as "a Fidonet mailer designed to operate via TCP/IP networks", and as a way to make "efficient utilization of TCP/IP protocol suite as a transport layer in FTN-based (Fido Technology Network) networks." Instead of a modem call, one node connects to another over the internet and the two exchange queued mail and file bundles.

The idea underneath is store-and-forward networking: no central server, just a web of peers that pass traffic along on a schedule. It is a different shape from the always-on, request-and-response internet most developers know. The README is brief and does not explain the protocol or configuration. The linked FAQ and manuals, in English and Russian, are where the detail lives. A community with echomail areas and mirrors still seems to surround it.
entry.install:
brew install binkd
# The brief documents a source build instead: git clone https://github.com/pgul/binkd, cp mkfls/unix/* . then ./configure && make
# Running it usefully needs a binkd.cfg and, in practice, a FidoNet-style node or a peer to connect to.

try_this.what_happens: Fetches the source, which is the install route the README documents for UNIX.
After building, shows what make install would do without touching your system.
Builds binkd for a different install directory instead of the default /usr/local.

entry.whats_unique: It is a working piece of FidoNet infrastructure, carrying pre-internet store-and-forward mail over TCP/IP, with manuals in both Russian and English.
entry.caveats: The README is thin on configuration, the status is unclear with no releases listed, and the linked manuals are old, covering 0.9.2 and 0.9.9.
